study_identification.title: A 10-Year Longitudinal Study of Brain Cortical Thickness in People with First-Episode Psychosis Using Normative Models

study_characteristics.study_objective: To characterize the temporal evolution of cortical correlates of psychosis and their associations with symptoms over a 10-year period using normative modeling. The study aimed to map the associations between brain cortical abnormalities and clinical symptoms over the longer term in people with first-episode psychosis.

site_effect_handling_detail.supporting_text: To account for site and scanner effects, we used the Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) approach for normative modeling, which efficiently accommodates inter-site variation and provides computational scaling, which is useful for multi-cohort and longitudinal studies with data from different scanners. We estimated a normative model for each region of interest (ROI, n = 150) in the Freesurfer Destrieux atlas, using HBR with age as a covariate, and sex and scanner id as batch effects, to predict CT. This accommodated multisite pooling using transfer learning and comparisons across scanners. ... Importantly, as HBR fits site-specific intercepts and slopes, the resulting normative trajectory might not be linear across the lifespan, but rather piecewise linear.
site_effect_handling_detail.location: Main paper, Methods section, Normative Modeling

model_origin_detail.answer: Reference normative models trained on 40,435 participants from 77 sites (95% healthy controls) using publicly available datasets. Models were then adapted to 3 Oslo scanners using transfer learning with held-out cross-sectional CTRL data from these scanners (n=790: TOP15 n=103, TOP3T n=294, TOP3T-GE n=393). See Kia et al. (2020, 2022) for detailed methods.

clinical_dataset.answer: TOP (Thematically Organized Psychosis) study; longitudinal first-episode sub-study at University of Oslo and Oslo University Hospital

diseases_studied.answer: First-episode psychosis (Schizophrenia spectrum disorders including schizophrenia, schizophreniform disorders, and schizoaffective disorder)

clinical_groups_n.answer: SCZ: 79 (baseline); 67 (12 months); 23 (10 years). Breakdown by diagnosis: schizophrenia n=57 (72%); schizophreniform n=18 (23%); schizoaffective n=4 (5%)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score (individual deviation scores from normative model for each ROI and timepoint); extreme deviation threshold defined as |z| > 2.0

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: Linear Mixed Effects (LME) models were used to test: (1) effects of diagnosis, time, age, sex, and diagnosis×time interaction on deviation scores across 150 ROIs; (2) associations between cortical deviations and PANSS scores (total, general, positive, negative) with time×deviation interaction. Non-parametric Wilcoxon tests compared proportions of extreme deviations between groups. Multiple comparison correction used Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (α=0.05). Key findings: significant conditional main effects of diagnosis and time×diagnosis interactions in distributed cortical network; anterior cingulate associated with PANSS total and general; left insula and orbitofrontal regions associated with PANSS negative; significant interaction between time and left posterior lateral sulcus on PANSS negative.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Patients with first-episode psychosis showed widespread negative cortical thickness deviations at baseline that attenuated over 10 years, concurrent with symptom reduction, not supporting a simple neurodegenerative model of schizophrenia.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: LME models revealed significant conditional main effects of diagnosis and time×diagnosis interactions in a distributed network of lateral temporal, parietal, and frontal regions bilaterally. Patients showed more negative deviation scores at baseline (Cohen's d=-0.46 for median thickness) which attenuated over time (d=-0.43 at 12 months, d=-0.27 at 10 years). At baseline, patients had significantly more extreme negative deviations (|z|<-2) compared to controls (p=2.56×10⁻⁵, CL=66%), with 3 ROIs showing strongest effects: left superior temporal gyrus lateral (CV=0.19), left inferior frontal gyrus opercular (CV=0.18), and right superior temporal sulcus (CV=0.18). These differences became non-significant by 10-year follow-up. PANSS scores significantly decreased over time (p<0.001), particularly during the first year. The left anterior cingulate gyrus showed associations with PANSS total (coefficient=-4.0, p=0.003) and PANSS general (coefficient=-1.79, p=0.01). Left anterior insula (coefficient=-1.3, p=0.04), posterior lateral sulcus (coefficient=1.52, p=0.03), and medial orbital sulcus (coefficient=-1.42, p=0.02) were associated with PANSS negative scores. A significant time×deviation interaction was found for the left posterior lateral sulcus on PANSS negative (coefficient=0.28, p=0.047), indicating initial associations attenuated over time. Medication data showed predominantly second-generation antipsychotic use (62% baseline, 48% at 1 year, 17% at 10 years) with no medication in remaining patients (38%, 50%, 83% respectively). Registry data analyses found no significant attrition bias in contacts with healthcare system, PANSS scores, or deviation scores.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: 1) Potential recruitment and retention biases despite access to national registry data; authors acknowledge non-trivial challenges in ensuring representative recruitment in clinical cohorts. 2) Unable to directly test differential effects of first- vs second-generation antipsychotics due to very few participants taking first-generation medications. 3) Extreme cortical deviations may reflect not only schizophrenia-related pathology but also noise, artifacts, medications, co-morbidities, or lifestyle factors, though QC procedures speak against this. 4) Moderate sample size at third timepoint (n=23 patients, n=77 controls); retention rate 38.3% for patients at 10 years, though effect size analyses suggest attenuation is not solely due to sample reduction. 5) Different scanners across waves may have influenced findings despite validated normative modeling framework. 6) Findings considered preliminary and await replication in other cohorts. 7) Lack of neurodevelopmental phase data prevents direct inference about neurodevelopmental antecedents of schizophrenia. 8) Sample likely enriched for favorable trajectories since good-outcome first-episode patients leave treatment services.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: This study demonstrates that transfer learning from large-scale reference normative models can enable meaningful comparisons of MRI features across different scanners in longitudinal studies. The findings provide preliminary evidence for cortical associations with longitudinal clinical outcomes in schizophrenia. The authors suggest that deviations from normative models offer a promising avenue to develop biomarkers to track clinical trajectories over time. The attenuation of cortical differences over time, together with symptom reduction, challenges simple neurodegenerative accounts of schizophrenia and may reflect the predominance of favorable clinical trajectories in long-term follow-up studies. The study also successfully used national registry data (Norwegian National Patient Registry) to assess potential attrition bias, finding no significant differences in healthcare contacts between retained and dropped-out patients.

general_notes.general_notes: This is a rare long-term (10-year) longitudinal neuroimaging study of first-episode psychosis with 3 timepoints (baseline, 12 months, 10 years). The study enrolled patients from October 27, 2004 to October 17, 2012. The study used 3 different MRI scanners sequentially without temporal overlap: 1.5T Siemens Magnetom Sonata (76% baseline, 72% 12-month, 6% 10-year), 3T GE Signa HDxT (5% baseline, 4% 12-month, 0% 10-year), and 3T GE Discovery 750 (19% baseline, 24% 12-month, 94% 10-year). The complete list of 77 sites and full dataset names in the reference normative model training set were not provided in detail; the paper states data came from 'mostly publicly available datasets' and references prior work (Wolfers et al. 2021). The sample was augmented by including additional CTRL from other TOP sub-studies on the same scanners to improve normative model fit. Inclusion criteria: age 18-53 for patients, 13-56 for controls; Scandinavian language fluency; IQ>70; no severe head trauma. First-episode defined as first adequate treatment for psychosis within last 12 months and no prior antipsychotic treatment >12 weeks. The study used DSM-IV SCID-I for diagnosis. National registry data (ICD-10 F01-F99) was used to track healthcare contacts as proxy for illness severity. Adaptation samples for transfer learning: TOP15 (n=103, age 36.6±10.3, 42.7% male), TOP3T (n=294, age 31.2±7.7, 48.8% male), TOP3T-GE (n=393, age 33.3±11.1, 49.8% male). The study found no significant differences in sex distribution at any timepoint, and Mann-Whitney U tests showed no significant differences in PANSS scores or healthcare contacts between retained and dropped-out patients. GLMM with binomial family found no significant effects of PANSS or deviation scores on attrition status. The paper notes that findings are discordant with neurodegenerative models and are more consistent with favorable clinical trajectories being overrepresented in long-term follow-up due to good-outcome patients leaving treatment services.
